earlier_scan.source_named: Retired glottocode: Sara Dunjo [koj] merged into Sara Kaba Naa [kwv] (ISO CR 2014-030); Glottolog lists no references.

new_statements.quote: 1.3 Tone. Like the Sara Languages, Na has three level tones: high, mid and low: ká 'so that, for', kō 'already', ɓà 'rainy season'. Tone-bearing phonemes are vowels and sonorant consonants when they are in final position. When a morpheme contains a sequence of identical vowels with distinct tones, or when a sonorant consonant closes a syllable, complex tones occur [...] Of the nine possible combinations, Mid-Low is not found. High-Low, which is very rare in the Sara languages with native morphemes, is common in Na, and is frequently used in verb conjugations.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Na (incl. its Dunje/Dunjo dialect area around Kyabé) is described as a three-level register tone language (H, M, L, with contours on VV sequences and coda sonorants); the description contains no statement of any kind about word stress or accent, so no stress position can be extracted. Only incidental prominence-adjacent remark: morpheme-final vowels of lexical morphemes are phonetically longer, vowel length not phonemic (§1.2).
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; tonal alternations (H > HL phrase-finally, LL > LH before kō, M > MH before clause marker nē) described in §1.4.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical tone on morphemes/words; nothing on word- or phrase-level stress. Intro was reviewed by Jim Roberts (SIL / Univ. N'Djamena).
new_statements.identity_note: sara1320 'Sara Dunjo' [koj] is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid: ISO 639-3 CR 2014-030 merged koj into Sara Kaba Náà [kwv] (Glottolog sara1321), where 'Dunje' is listed as a dialect alongside Banga, Na and Tie. All accessible description is of Na (Sara Kaba Na) as spoken around Kyabé, principal consultant Kodé Koutou; Keegan notes (fn. 3, p. ix) that little dialectal variation is included, and the Dunjo are mentioned only as an ethnic group in a dictionary example (s.v. ndājó). Any catalog entry should be filed under sara1321 / kwv, not under the retired code.

new_statements.quote: [2a] Tone is both lexical and grammatical (see §§ 4, 8, 9). In the languages so far analysed for tone (BONGO, BAKA, MOROKODO, KRESH, YULU, KARA, SARA MBAI and to some extent BAGIRMI) three levels have been noted [...] There is great variation between dialects, and even between individuals, in the tone patterns of words, especially when spoken in isolation. [2b. Stress] Stress is normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words, and invariably so when the second syllable contains a semi-mute vowel. Occasionally stress is heard on the second syllable, when the first one contains a central vowel. Stevenson records stress on the second syllable in BAGIRMI kala [scanned; Google Books snippet 'k ;lá', i.e. a central first vowel], snake, for instance. 3. Word Shape [...]

new_statements.relation_note: No catalog record for sara1320. The one statement held by the project (Keegan & Koutou 2015, Na: three level tones, no stress statement) is compatible: Tucker & Bryan also give three tone levels for the group and ADD a stress placement (normally initial in disyllables, vowel-quality-conditioned exceptions). Caveat on scope: it is a generalisation over the Bongo-Bagirmi group drawn mainly from Bongo, Baka, Morokodo, Kresh, Yulu, Kara, Sara Mbai and Bagirmi; Sara Kaba appears in the chapter's comparative word tables (p. 73 fragment 'SARA KABA na') but Dunjo itself was not seen named in any fragment (an archive.org full-text check for 'Dunjo'/'Kaba' could not be run today: archive.org deferred…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement for the Bongo-Bagirmi languages (the chapter that cites SARA KABA and SARA MBAI among its members): three level tones, lexical and grammatical; word stress normally falls on the FIRST syllable of disyllabic words, obligatorily so when the second syllable has a 'semi-mute' (reduced) vowel; stress may shift to the second syllable when the first syllable has a central vowel (example from Bagirmi). Not a statement made specifically about Sara Dunjo / Sara Kaba Na, which is not among the languages the authors say were analysed for tone.
new_statements.exceptions: stress on the second syllable 'occasionally', when the first syllable contains a central vowel (Stevenson's Bagirmi 'snake' example); statement restricted to disyllabic words.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan 1966 treat the 'Bongo-Bagirmi' group as a unit; 'SARA KABA' (the Sara Kaba cluster of south-eastern Chad, into whose member Sara Kaba Naa [kwv] the retired Sara Dunjo [koj] was merged by ISO CR 2014-030) is cited in the chapter's comparative word tables (p. 73 fragment); 'Dunjo' was not seen in any fragment and could not be full-text-checked today (archive.org deferred). The 1956 Handbook by the same authors (a different work, held by the project separately) is the one that lists Dunjo (p. 57). Keegan & Koutou 2015 describe Na (Sara Kaba Naa) specifically.
